pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Building shade from the sun

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no KS1 'energy' content, so no direct UK science statutory match; the design-make-evaluate element lives in KS1 Design & Technology, and the testing reasoning in KS1 'Working scientifically' (performing simple tests; gathering and recording data to answer a question).

- **Standards — US NATIONAL (NGSS):** K-PS3-2 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]' (an engineering PE, asterisked); clarification examples — umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'. NGSS-anchored. Builds directly on 'Sunlight warms things up'.

- **Operational details:** An ENGINEERING-DESIGN topic: children use simple [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2] (umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol) that REDUCES [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2], then test it by comparing the shaded spot with an unshaded one (relative warmer/cooler). The science is the prior observation (sun warms surfaces); the task is design→build→test, kept qualitative — no degrees, no materials-science theory.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/procedural, age 5-6, pre-readers).
bestPractices: Frame a real problem the child cares about: 'the slide / the sandpit / our toy gets too hot in the sun — can you build something to keep it cool?' so the build has a purpose.
Run a genuine design loop at a 5-6 level: choose materials, build a shade, TEST by feeling/measuring the shaded vs sunny spot, then improve one thing (bigger? thicker? angled to block the sun?).
Make the test a fair comparison without the jargon: same object, one spot shaded by the structure and one left in the sun, checked at the same time — cooler under the shade is the evidence it worked.
Let material choice matter: compare a see-through/mesh cover with a solid opaque one so children notice that blocking the sunlight (not just covering) is what cools the area.
Connect cause to design: because the SUN warms the area (prior topic), the structure works by getting between the sun and the area — position and coverage matter, not just size.
keyRepresentations: The problem object (hot slide / sandpit / a chocolate or ice cube to protect) plus a build kit of cloths, card, sticks, pegs.
A design-loop at picture level: think → build → test (feel/measure) → make it better.
A shaded-vs-sunny comparison of the same spot, with warm/cool faces as the result.
Real exemplars: umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol, sun-sail — things that get between the sun and the ground.
commonMisconceptions: 'Any cover works the same' — a see-through or holey cover still lets the sun warm the area; blocking the sunlight is what matters (opacity/coverage).
'Shade makes cold' — carried from the prior topic; the structure doesn't make cold, it stops the sun reaching and warming the area.
Thinking the structure must be big or tall rather than POSITIONED to block the sun's path to the area.
Treating the first build as finished — missing that testing and improving (iteration) is the task.
Judging success by looks ('it's a nice tent') rather than by the evidence (is the shaded spot actually cooler than the sunny one?).

learn.summary: For children aged 5–6, build-and-test a shade structure that reduces the warming effect of sunlight on a spot (aligned to NGSS K-PS3-2 engineering design). The central learning is a hands-on design loop: choose materials, build a cover (umbrella/canopy/tent/parasol), position it between the sun and a target spot, then test by comparing the shaded spot with an unshaded one at the same time. Key insight: blocking the sunlight (opacity and position), not just covering, is what keeps the area cooler. Check which cover works by looking at the shadow or bright patch on the ground — never by looking toward the sun. An on-screen design bench and reference/check activities support the loop and fair-comparison logic, but the real outdoor build-and-test is what the standard requires.

activities.title: Build, position and test a real shade
feedback: If sunlight still lands on the spot: 'Is your spot still in a bright patch of sunlight? Move your cover until your spot is in its shadow — shade is wherever the light is blocked.'
If the child declares success without comparing: 'How do you know it's cooler? Let's check a covered spot and a sunny spot side by side at the same time and feel/measure both.'

If a see-through or thin cover is used: 'Put each cover over the spot and look at the GROUND — which one still shows a bright patch, and which casts a dark shadow? Then test which cover keeps the spot coolest compared with a sunny spot. (Never look up at the sun through the cover.)'

If the build is treated as finished after one try: 'Change just one thing — maybe make it bigger or use a thicker cloth — and test again, comparing the shaded and sunny spots to see if it gets cooler.'
activities.rationale: K-PS3-2 calls for [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]. This activity includes choosing and assembling real materials, testing their coverage, and revising the build. Comparing matched shaded and unshaded spots after the same elapsed time provides evidence about reduced warming.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-2 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]'); clarification examples umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'.
Young children commonly think any cover works the same and that shade 'makes cold'; blocking the sunlight (opacity/position) is what reduces warming.
learnerActions: Start from a real problem the child cares about: 'the slide / sandpit / our toy gets too hot in the sun — can you build something to keep it cool?'

Offer a kit — cloths, card, sticks, pegs — and ask the child to choose a material and build a cover (umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol) over a target spot (a thermometer, a toy, or something to keep cool such as a chocolate or ice cube on the ground).
Have the child place the cover so it sits BETWEEN the sun and the spot; look at the ground and move the cover until the target spot is in the cover's shadow instead of bright sunlight.

Set up a fair comparison: two of the same kind of spot that start out alike, one shaded by the structure and one left in the sun, then check both after the same time has passed, by careful feel or with a relative thermometer.
Improve one thing and re-test (bigger? thicker/more opaque? angled to block the sun's path?), then judge success from the evidence: is the shaded spot cooler than the sunny one?
activities.intendedInsight: A shade works by getting between the sun and the area and blocking the sunlight; you can tell it worked because the shaded spot is cooler than a matching sunny spot checked at the same time, not because it looks nice.

activities.title: On-screen shade-design bench (companion for the design loop)
feedback: When an open net still lets light reach the spot: 'The sun is coming through the holes, so that spot keeps warming — compare it with the solid cover over the same time.'
When the solid cover keeps the spot cooler: 'Over the test the covered spot stayed cooler while the bare spot kept warming — your shade blocked the sunlight.'
Using the results strip: 'Look back at your marks — which build kept the spot coolest?'
activities.rationale: An interactive design bench rehearses the design-loop and the fair-comparison logic on screen and makes the blocking-vs-covering idea visible through an open cover that lets light through. It is a companion to, not a replacement for, the physical build-and-test the standard requires.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-2 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]'); clarification examples umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'.
Young children commonly think any cover works the same and that shade 'makes cold'; blocking the sunlight (opacity/position) is what reduces warming.
learnerActions: Show a toy on a sunny slide (or a spot on a play area) and a kit of covers — cloth, open net, card — that the child can drag over the spot, resize and position relative to the sun.

Run a 'sun test' over time with two probes that start alike, one covered and one uncovered: across the test the uncovered spot keeps warming (warm face) while the covered spot stays cooler (cool face), so the difference grows over elapsed time rather than appearing instantly.
Use a 'change one thing' control and a persistent results strip that keeps each test's hit/miss mark on screen, so a pre-reader can read their own evidence and judge 'did it work?'.

Have the child try an open see-through net first and watch it still let light reach the spot so the spot keeps warming, then swap to a solid opaque cloth and re-test over the same time to see the covered spot stay cooler (note a tight weave may only partly reduce warming).

Keep all prompts picture + audio and all temperature language relative (warmer/cooler, no degrees); read which build worked from the shadow under the cover and the two probes, not by looking toward the sun.
activities.intendedInsight: Blocking the sun's light — not merely covering — is what keeps the spot cooler, and the structure must sit between the sun and the area; you confirm it by comparing covered and uncovered probes over the same time across repeated tests.

activities.title: Explore real shade exemplars (reference)
feedback: 'Where does this umbrella block the sun? Which patch of ground stays in the shadow and cool?'
'What do the tent, canopy and umbrella all do to the sunlight?'
activities.rationale: Exemplar scenes build the concept with familiar objects and picture+audio support, but they are reference material: a picture cannot deliver the design, build or test actions that are the core of this engineering topic.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-2 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]'); clarification examples umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'.
learnerActions: Share a tappable or picture scene of real shade structures — umbrella, tent, canopy, sun-sail — and reveal the cooler area beneath each with 'this blocks the sun so it's cooler underneath' in picture + audio.
Ask the child to point out where each structure sits relative to the sun and which patch of ground it keeps in shadow.
Connect to the prior idea that the sun warms the area: because the sun warms the ground, a structure helps by getting between the sun and the spot.
activities.intendedInsight: Real shade structures all work in the same way — they get between the sun and the ground to block the light and cast a shadow — so position and coverage matter, not just size.

activities.title: Quick check — which cover keeps it coolest? (recognition)
feedback: If the see-through cover is chosen as coolest: 'Look at the ground under each cover — the sun still makes a bright patch under the see-through one. Which cover casts a dark shadow on the ground?'
If correct: 'Yes — that cover blocks the sun and casts a dark shadow, so the spot stays cooler.'
activities.rationale: A short picture+audio check can confirm the blocking-vs-covering idea, but recognition-only questions do not elicit the independent design-build-test-improve work that is the objective, so use it only alongside the build activity.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly think any cover works the same and that shade 'makes cold'; blocking the sunlight (opacity/position) is what reduces warming.
learnerActions: Pose a picture + audio question such as 'which shade keeps it coolest?' or 'is the spot under the umbrella warmer or cooler?' comparing a see-through cover with a solid one.
Ask the child to match a shade structure to the cooler shaded area beneath it, looking at which cover casts a dark shadow on the ground.
Keep temperature language relative (warmer/cooler) and provide adult/audio support for pre-readers.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid, well-positioned cover casts a dark shadow and keeps the spot cooler than a see-through or poorly placed one.

constraints: This is an engineering-design (procedural) topic for ages 5–6: the required learning is designing, building and testing a real structure with tools and materials, kept qualitative — no degrees and no materials-science theory.
Keep the test a fair comparison without jargon: same object/spot, one shaded and one in the sun, checked at the same time; cooler under the shade is the evidence it worked.

Observe shade safely by looking at the cast shadow or bright patch on the GROUND; never ask a child to look toward the sun or hold material up to their eyes to see whether they can see the sun through it.
Shade reduces warming over time rather than instantly cooling an already-hot surface; compare the shaded and unshaded spots over the same elapsed time, not a magic instant drop.
Open see-through/net covers let light through, but a tightly woven cover may only partly reduce warming; compare actual outcomes rather than assuming mesh always fails and opaque always succeeds.

On-screen benches, exemplar scenes and quizzes are scaffolds/companions for the design loop and comparison logic; they do not substitute for the physical build-and-test and the genuine cool of a real shaded patch, so pair them with the real outdoor activity.
Recognition-only questions check understanding but do not demonstrate independent design, build or iteration.
Address the 'shade makes cold' idea: the structure does not make cold, it stops the sun reaching and warming the area.
Address the 'any cover works' idea: a see-through or holey cover still lets the sun warm the spot; opacity and position matter.
Emphasise positioning over size: the cover must intercept the sun's path to the spot; a tall or large structure that is not in the sun's path to the spot still lets light land on it.
Treat iteration as part of the task: change one thing and re-test rather than stopping at the first build; judge success by evidence, not by looks.
Needed for the real activity: a shade-building kit (cloths, card, sticks/pegs) and a sunny spot to test shaded vs unshaded by hand or with a relative thermometer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IOP Spark source on children's ideas (any cover works the same; shade 'makes cold') is marked unverified in the source row; treat the misconception framing as guidance pending verification.

The original assessment error-pattern nextMove instructed holding candidate materials 'up to the sun' to see through them; corrected across the guidance to a ground-shadow check for child safety, since looking toward the sun is unsafe for young children.

Mesh/open-cover outcomes depend on weave and setup; the original row framed a mesh cover as simply 'failing' — softened to an open net letting light through while noting a tight weave may only partly reduce warming.

The original row asserts '3D adds handling burden for young children' and that an in-role dialogue 'doesn't develop the engineering task'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established efficacy findings; a 3D build or a conversation could still support motivation or explanation. Narrowed accordingly and not stated as universal laws.

The original recommendation leaned on a specific digital bench as the primary vehicle; corrected emphasis so the real hands-on build-and-test is primary and the bench is a companion, consistent with the row's own catalog-gap note.

Outdoor testing results depend on real conditions (cloud, time of day, sun's movement); keep comparisons same-time and same-spot, and note the shade may not cover the spot later as the sun moves (per the assessment probes).

probeDeeper: Show me where the sunlight is still getting through — can you change your shade so it doesn't?
How will you prove your shade made it cooler, and that it wasn't just cooler there anyway?
It's cloudy now — will your shade still make much difference? Why or why not?
If the sun moves across the sky, will your shade still cover the spot this afternoon?
assess.correctAnswer: Builds a cover that physically blocks the sunlight from reaching the spot — positioned between the sun and the target, opaque enough to cast real shade — then tests by comparing the temperature or feel of the shaded spot against an unshaded spot, judging it worked if the shaded one is cooler.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a structure but doesn't place it to block the sun's path — a wall beside the spot, or a roof full of gaps ('it's a shelter' but light still lands on the spot).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child look for the bright patch on the ground and move the cover until that patch is gone; shade is wherever the light is blocked.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching where the cover goes — sunlight still reaches the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Declares it worked without comparing to an unshaded spot ('it's cooler, I just know').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Set up two spots side by side — one covered, one not — and compare by touch or thermometer; scaffold the fair comparison rather than reteaching shade.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Skips the test or offers no control comparison when asked to show how they'll check.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a see-through or very thin material and expects full shade ('the clear plastic will shade it').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold candidate materials up to the sun and pick the one you can't see through; test which casts the darkest shadow.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The material lets light through and the target stays bright.

responseLevels.gap: Builds a structure that doesn't block the light (gaps, wrong position, transparent), or claims success with no comparison.
responseLevels.full: Positions an opaque cover to intercept the sun's light so the target is fully shaded, then tests by comparing the shaded and unshaded temperature or feel and judges effectiveness on that evidence.
responseLevels.partial: Blocks the sunlight and produces shade, but tests loosely — no clear comparison to an unshaded spot, or can't say what 'worked' should look like.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are cloth, card, sticks and pegs. Make something that will keep this spot of ground (with a thermometer or toy on it) cooler in the sunshine. Set it up, then show me how you'll check whether it worked. [Watch: does the child place the cover BETWEEN the sun and the spot, block the light fully, and compare the shaded spot with a sunny one to test?]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who grasps that shade means blocking the sun's path (places the cover to intercept the light and checks against a sunny control) from one who builds a decorative 'house' without blocking the light, or declares success with no comparison.
